In the criminal justice system, job market failures are considered especially heinous. On LinkedIn, the candidates who investigate these scams are members of an elite squad. These are their stories. DUN DUN.

Admit it, you read that with the accent! On a more serious note, my sister Eve B.  had a bad experience on LinkedIn while applying for a job.

At first, nothing out of the ordinary, she applied for the job just like she had for others on the platform. Shortly after, she got a direct text message on her phone to schedule an interview. No prior call, no official email.

First 🚩: what serious company operates via a simple text message?
Then again, since so few companies actually reply, when you do get a response, you don't always pay attention. So she scheduled a phone interview.

When trying to prepare for the interview, she started digging, and red flags began popping up:
🚩 Shaddy website: the job offer led to a website with zero legal notices or actual contact details.
🚩 Suspicious content: the site looked like AI-generated content, no edit.
🚩 Almost empty LinkedIn page: very little activity, and the only two employee profiles linked to the page strongly resembled fake profiles.

The more she searched, the more the inconsistencies piled up. That’s when she understood the scam: an attempt at identity theft.

In France, the hiring process requires an ID document, a Social Security certificate, and bank details (RIB) to draw up the employment contract... everything needed to steal your identity.

How to protect yourself (and others):
1️⃣ Add a watermark to your documents: Before sending any official document to a recruiter, overlay it with a watermark stating the recipient and the date. The government provides a free and secure tool: FiligraneFacile.

2️⃣ Report scams: We directly reported this fake platform on PHAROS, the official portal for reporting illegal content.

What about you? Have you ever been targeted by a scam?"

The companies winning with AI right now aren't the ones buying the most tools. They're the ones who shifted from asking "Can AI do this?" to "Which workflows should AI own, and where do humans stay in charge?"

We're past the chatbot era. The latest shift is agentic AI — systems that don't just answer questions but plan multi-step work, use tools, check their own output, and escalate to a human when the stakes rise. Gartner named multi-agent systems a top strategic trend for 2026. Enterprise AI spending is on track to cross $300B globally, with nearly 40% of work activities becoming automatable.

But here's what most leaders get wrong: they automate tasks when they should be automating workflows. Drafting an email is a task. Receiving a lead, checking fit, researching context, drafting a reply, logging the result, and setting a follow-up — that's a workflow. The value compounds at the workflow level.

The playbook for companies that get it right:
1. Start with strategy, not tools. Map the workflow before you pick the AI.
2. Treat AI agents like junior colleagues with access controls — clear job description, limited permissions, review path, and a record of what they did.
3. Build exception queues. Your agent must know when to stop and ask for help.
4. Keep humans in charge of contracts, payments, hiring, and high-stakes decisions.
5. Measure what matters: completion time, error rate, human edits, and business impact.

The real risk in 2026 isn't that AI replaces your team. It's that your competitors build AI-native workflows faster than you do — and your team is still doing manually what their agents handle before lunch.

The question isn't whether to deploy AI agents. It's whether you're designing the right boundaries around them.

Your recruitment AI can break the rules before it rejects anyone.

Imagine a head of HR at a 2,000-person company who is buying an AI sourcing tool. The demo shows sharper shortlists. Nobody asks where the candidate data came from.

We call this borrowed compliance. When you buy the tool, its data practices become part of your hiring process, yet you never see them. The risk is not only in what the tool decides. It is in how the tool was built and fed.

In November 2024 the UK's ICO published the outcomes of its audits of providers of AI recruitment tools. Its auditors made 296 recommendations and 42 advisory notes. The findings were specific. Some tools let recruiters filter out candidates by protected characteristics. Others inferred gender or ethnicity from a name. The ICO judged those inferences too inaccurate to monitor bias, and found they were often processed without a lawful basis or the candidate's knowledge. Some tools also collected far more personal information than they needed.

The EU treats the same use case with more weight. AI used for recruitment and selection is listed as high-risk under the AI Act, and the high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Employers using such a system are deployers, and deployers carry their own duties, including human oversight by people with real authority. The UK and the EU differ in law. They agree on the question: can you explain how this tool treats a candidate?

Before signing, ask three questions, and write the answers into the contract. Where did the candidate data come from, and on what lawful basis? What does the tool infer about candidates, and can that be switched off? Who can overrule a ranking, and is the override recorded?

If you cannot get answers to those three questions before you sign, that is where we start.

#Recruitment #AIGovernance #ICO

The boardroom always gets weird when smart people start debating whether a machine has a soul.
By then the invoice is already due, the policy is already written, and somebody's job just got routed through a server rack with better branding than judgment.

People love the magic trick. They want to argue about "consciousness" because it sounds profound and keeps them safely away from accountability. Cute. The real issue is behavior. What the system is allowed to decide, who signed off on it, and which ordinary man gets buried under the paperwork when it goes sideways.

A company does not get a pass because the spreadsheet was automated. A lender does not get moral amnesty because the denial came from code. A leadership team still owns the decision, even if they dressed it up in sleek language and parked it inside a deck with twelve colors and no courage.

Picture a founder who hires a polished executive to run operations. The executive smiles, misses payroll, mangles contracts, and blames the software. Every man in the room knows the truth. Bad outcomes with a polished explanation still wreck lives.

I say that as a guy who enjoys efficiency a little too much. If a dashboard can clear my calendar and tighten a forecast, my inner operator starts grinning like a fool. Then I remember that convenience is a petty little idol when it starts replacing judgment, responsibility, and plain old backbone.

The coming fight over AI has very little to do with philosophy and everything to do with stewardship. Men should care because behavior shapes paychecks, truth, hiring, lending, security, and the kind of world we hand the next man coming up behind us. A tool with no character in the hands of people with no limits becomes a quiet tyrant.

Ask one hard question every time AI shows up in the room. Who answers when this thing harms someone?

Because somewhere a man is staring at a bank statement, a contract, or a rejection notice, and he deserves a human name on the decision.

Faith. Finance. Focus.
Strong Men. Strong Homes. Strong Businesses.

Option 1: The Comprehensive Guide (Best for saves and shares)

Headline: A 200 OK response doesn't always mean your API is working correctly. 🛑

We've all been there. The endpoint returns a 200, but the data is wrong, the system is slow, or a downstream service is broken.

As this great infographic by ByteByteGo shows, true API reliability goes far beyond a basic ping. Here are the 9 essential types of API testing every developer and QA engineer should know:

1️⃣ Smoke Testing: The basic health check. Does it return a 200 OK? (Basic availability).
2️⃣ Functional Testing: Does the output match the requirements? Validating behavior against expected results.
3️⃣ Contract Testing: Do the Consumer and Provider agree on the data format? Ensures requests/responses match the schema.
4️⃣ Integration Testing: Does the API play nicely with others? Validating workflows across dependent services (e.g., Order ➡️ Inventory ➡️ Payment).
5️⃣ Regression Testing: Did your new code break old features? Comparing v1 to v2.
6️⃣ Load Testing: Can it handle the expected traffic? Measuring latency under a steady-state load.
7️⃣ Stress Testing: Where is the breaking point? Ramping up traffic until throttling or 5xx errors occur.
8️⃣ Security Testing: Is it locked down? Verifying auth, access control, and data protection.
9️⃣ Fuzzing Testing: How does it handle garbage? Probing malformed inputs and edge cases to uncover hidden bugs.

Building a resilient system means layering these tests. You wouldn't ship a car without testing the brakes, the engine, AND the crash safety.

One of them happened to be hiring. They interviewed him. He got the job.

That call made me about 10 grand.

But, it was one call out of 400 that week.

Wouldn't it be great to make 5 calls instead of 400, and get 5 jobs on?

Last year I had an amazing supply chain candidate. A specialist in contract manufacturing.

I didn't open a directory. I had AI research every competitor that also uses contract manufacturing, then find the right people and their contact details.

Then I picked up the phone.

5 interviews.

Blind calling relies on luck.

Calling smart means you make your own.

The difference is what you know before you dial. 

Who's likely to need this person and why. What to say when they pick up.

Your recruiters are already good on the phone.

So if you run a recruitment team, what's the point of them calling blind?

Redesign the workflow. Put AI agents on the prospecting. Let your recruiters make 5 quality calls instead of 400.

Or better still, 400 smart ones.

1️⃣ "Nobody's hiring contractors any more." 

The RECs index for IT contractor demand hit 52.7 in August 2026 (anything above 50 means growth). That's its highest reading since April 2023. 

2️⃣ "AI is just a buzzword in job adverts." 

According to IT Jobs Watch, 5,341 UK contract jobs cited AI in the six months to 2 October 2026, up from 1,606 a year earlier. That's 9.73% of all UK contract jobs, up from 4.85%. 

3️⃣ "Put AI on your CV and your day rate will soar." 

The median quoted rate for contract jobs citing AI was £560 a day. But adding "ChatGPT" to your skills list wont get you there. 

4️⃣ "AI is the only skill that matters now." 

Recruiters are still reporting shortages of contractors in cybersecurity, cloud computing, software engineering and security-cleared IT. 

AI isn't replacing good contractors. But contractors who couple real domain expertise with practical, provable AI delivery are leading the charge. 

Are you seeing more AI in your contract briefs, or is it mostly buzzwords?

🔎 **5 industry signals from this week that leaders should pay attention to**

Here are the trends I’m seeing repeatedly across strategy conversations, earnings commentary, and product moves:

1) **AI is shifting from “pilot mode” to workflow integration**  
   Companies are prioritizing use cases tied to revenue, margin, or cycle-time reduction—not just experimentation.  
   **Action:** Audit your top 3 AI initiatives and require a clear business KPI for each (cost saved, hours reduced, conversion improved).

2) **Cost discipline is now “smart efficiency,” not broad cuts**  
   Teams are protecting customer-facing and growth functions while automating back-office-heavy work.  
   **Action:** Identify one process per department that can be redesigned (not just reduced) using automation + clearer ownership.

3) **Cybersecurity is being treated as a business continuity issue**  
   Rising attacks and stricter customer/vendor requirements are pushing security into board-level risk planning.  
   **Action:** Run a 60-minute tabletop exercise this month: “If core systems go down for 24 hours, what breaks first?”

4) **Procurement is becoming a strategic lever again**  
   Vendor consolidation and contract renegotiation are accelerating, especially in SaaS and logistics.  
   **Action:** Review your top 10 vendor contracts for overlap, shelfware, and renewal timing before budgets lock.

5) **Talent strategy is moving toward capability depth, not headcount growth**  
   Organizations are investing in upskilling and role redesign to close skill gaps faster than hiring alone can.  
   **Action:** Build a “skills heatmap” for your team and align L&D spending to your 2 most critical capability gaps.

---

If you had to prioritize just **one** of these in Q4 planning, which would it be?

Embaucher un salarié étranger : votre bonne foi ne se présume pas. Elle se prouve.

« Il m'a présenté son titre de séjour, j'en ai gardé une copie. » Après un contrôle, cette défense ne suffit pas.

- L'interdiction vise l'embauche, mais aussi le maintien en poste (art. L. 8251-1 C. trav.). Un titre qui expire en cours de contrat vous place en infraction.

- La vérification auprès du préfet est obligatoire, au moins 2 jours ouvrables avant l'embauche (art. R. 5221-41 et R. 5221-42).

- Les sanctions : 5 ans d'emprisonnement et 30 000 € d'amende par salarié concerné (art. L. 8256-2), plus une amende administrative pouvant dépasser 20 000 € par salarié, et 60 000 € en cas de réitération (art. L. 8253-1).

La conformité se construit avant le contrôle.

Vos dossiers résisteraient-ils à un contrôle demain ? 

#DroitDuTravail #RessourcesHumaines #Recrutement #DroitDesEtrangers #Dirigeants

Hiring a foreign employee in France: your good faith is not presumed. It has to be proven.

"He showed me his residence permit and I kept a copy." After an inspection, that defence is not enough.

- The prohibition covers hiring, but also keeping someone in post (art. L. 8251-1, French Labour Code). A permit that expires mid-contract puts you in breach.

- Verification with the Prefect is mandatory, at least 2 working days before the hire (art. R. 5221-41 and R. 5221-42).

- The penalties: 5 years' imprisonment and a €30,000 fine per employee concerned (art. L. 8256-2), plus an administrative fine that can exceed €20,000 per employee, and €60,000 for repeat breaches (art. L. 8253-1).

Compliance is built before the inspection.

Google just updated its guidance to say AI-generated content must be manually fact-checked before publishing. 
Titles, meta descriptions, schema and alt text included. 

Honestly? I read that and thought, you're only saying this now? 

Because this is what's happening on our side of the screen. Companies use AI to generate content, then decide the writer is no longer needed, or at least not full-time. Suddenly the role becomes contract or freelance, at lower pay, because AI does most of the work anyway.

No, technically, it doesn't. 
Someone still has to: 
→ know the audience and the business 
→ check every claim, stat and source 
→ fix what the tool got confidently wrong 
→ decide what the piece is actually trying to say 
→ make sure it still sounds like the brand and not like every other AI blog 

That is the job. It's skilled work, and it was never just writing. 

And when full-time roles do open up, many applications seem to go through ATS screening, which is also AI. A writer with real experience may never reach a human because the resume didn't match the right keywords. 

So we're undervalued before the work and filtered out before the interview. 

I'm not against AI. In fact, I use it, and it's useful for research, structure and first drafts. But pasting something in and typing "make it engaging" or "make it more human" isn't content drafting. Sorry mate, it just doesn't work that way. If it did, the internet wouldn't be full of content that reads the same.

One pattern stood out in this week’s software developer hiring posts: roles are named by a stack, but the real delivery gap is usually about ownership.
A full stack developer, Flutter developer, or contract software developer can add capacity. But if product decisions still pass through separate frontend, backend, cloud, and client handoffs, the roadmap may not move much faster.
In the mobile and web products I build, the useful engineer is often the person who can carry a slice from an unclear requirement to a working release, then explain the trade-offs along the way.
That is why I see a Senior Forward Deployment Engineer as more than a software developer hiring checkbox. It combines product engineering, implementation, and feedback from the real environment.
For a startup tech team working on SaaS development, MVP development, or an AI-powered product, hire for the gap you have now. Choose full-time, remote, or contract support deliberately. Keep ownership close to the product.
The best hire is not the longest skills list. It is the person who can reduce the next handoff.
What would you hire for first: stack depth or end-to-end ownership?

Candidates think AI scans their CV. 
1,000+ CVs later, I can tell you: I don't need AI.

It takes me 10 seconds.
In this exact order:

1. YOUR LATEST JOB TITLE
→ Does it match the role I'm hiring for?

2. YOUR TIMELINE 
→ How long did you stay? Is there a pattern?

3. YOUR LOCATION
→ Are you here, or about to be?

4. THE FIRST 5 BULLETS OF EACH ROLE
→ Are about impact or just tasks? 

5. IS YOUR EXPERIENCE RELEVANT FOR THIS JOB? 
→ If I have to work to find the match, I move on.

I've recruited for the last 8 years and trust me, it's not as complicated as you think. 

"You need to have a CV " ATS friendly"? 
No love, you need to have a CV "recruiter friendly", because that's who actually read it. 

Technology helps us, it doesn't replace anyone. 

So here 5 simple fix: 

1. Make sure your job title is in line with your application. 
2. Month and year on every role. Short stint? One line on why (contract, relocation).
3. Your current city at the top. If you're relocating, say WHEN.
4. Lead with your biggest result, not your daily tasks.
5. Use relevant experience to match the transferable skills. 

CV doesn't have to be perfect. 
It just needs to give a reason to call you. 

Don't overcomplicate it.

AI-linked roles have accounted for more than 750,000 new jobs in the US since 2023, according to LinkedIn estimates. The largest single category added 282,000 of them. 

Published job creation data only captures new roles being posted, and it misses every existing role being repositioned around AI work inside an enterprise. 

A bank is not only hiring AI engineers. It is moving data analysts, risk modellers, and internal software teams onto agent deployment. None of that shows up as a new job created. 

Deploying AI into a large organisation turns out to require an enormous amount of technical and services work. Someone has to build the applied product, integrate it into existing systems, handle governance, and then stay involved while it actually runs. 

That is why forward deployed engineers have become a standard line item in enterprise AI contracts, and why services firms are being built specifically around deployment. 

The India relevance here is direct. This deployment layer is exactly the work Indian IT services firms have delivered for three decades, and it is the reason the AI services opportunity is likely larger than the IT services market it is supposedly replacing. 

The jobs AI creates are harder to see than the ones it displaces. They sit inside companies rather than in headlines.

AI broke my design hiring process.
I'm glad it did. 👇

The quality of design assessments I receive has never been higher.

That's become the problem.

Every take-home now arrives polished: clean layouts, tidy flows, confident rationale. And I can no longer tell a strong designer from a strong prompt.

This isn't just a design problem. If you hire developers, writers, analysts or marketers, you're facing the same question:

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲'𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝘁?

We could have banned AI from our assessments. 
We did the opposite. My team uses it every day, so testing people without it would test the wrong thing.

Which leaves a harder question: if the output no longer separates people, what does?

Nobody has a settled answer yet, and there's no widely accepted framework. 
Here's where my thinking is right now:

1. The AI disclosure is the assessment. Show me which tools you used, what you asked for, what you kept, what you threw away, and why.

2. Editing is judgement. What someone rejected tells me more than what they shipped.

3. Setup over prompting. Did you write a clear spec so the AI could work on its own, or did you steer every step? We lean towards the first: define the problem well, then let the AI run. Spec-driven, not vibe coding.

4. Improve the system, don't just use it. I want people who make the team's AI setup better for everyone.

The live walkthrough is where it all shows. 
Polished screens with thin reasoning look fine on a slide and fall apart the moment you ask "why?"

I'd rather rebuild the process than pretend the old one still works.

🤔💬 So I'm curious:

𝗛𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘀: 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗔𝗜? 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲?

𝗝𝗼𝗯 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗸𝗲𝗿𝘀: 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲, 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝗱?
